cards.definitions: A NAND gate takes two bits u,v and outputs ¬(u∧v). A NAND formula is a rooted binary tree of such gates whose leaves are input bits, their negations or Boolean constants; depth is the largest number of gates on an input-to-output path. For c≥0, the source writes NDepth[c log₂n] for languages decided by uniform NAND formulas with depth at most (c+o(1))log₂n; the o(1) tends to zero as input length n grows. The coefficient c is therefore meaningful and is not hidden in O(log n). In Definition 1.5 a single random-access machine A receives n, an n-bit input x, and a binary address b describing a path from the root (0 for left, 1 for right). It must describe the gate at that address in time (log n)^O(1). The source calls this input-aware uniformity and says it can select subformulas using bits of x. Its displayed definition still denotes the formula by φ_n rather than φ_{n,x}; that distinction is left explicit here. Strict class containment means that some language belongs to the larger-depth class and to no formula family in the smaller-depth class. It is a separation of deterministic NAND computations, not a comparison of nondeterministic time bounds.
cards.answer_criterion: After fixing the source’s input-aware representation and coefficient range, prove strict containment for every required a<b without assuming that SAT or NTIME[n] has shallow NAND formulas, or refute that hierarchy in the same model. A lower bound for SAT alone, a conditional hierarchy, or a separation under a different uniformity notion does not settle it.

context_blocks.title: The paper’s hierarchy is conditional

references.title: Max Weight Independent Set in Sparse Graphs with No Long Claws
references.authors: Abrishami, Tara; Chudnovsky, Maria; Pilipczuk, Marcin; Rzążewski, Paweł

cards.definitions: The input is a finite undirected simple graph G=(V,E), with n=|V|, and integer weights w:V→N. An independent set I⊆V contains no adjacent pair, and its weight is Σ_{v∈I}w(v), with the empty set having weight zero. S_{t,t,t} is the tree formed by three paths of t edges sharing one common endpoint and otherwise having disjoint vertices; it has 3t+1 vertices and one degree-three center. An induced copy requires exactly the edges of that tree among its selected vertices. K_r is the complete graph on r vertices, so excluding it means every clique has size at most r−1. The algorithm is promised both exclusions. For each fixed t,r its running time must be at most n^{c(t,r)} times a constant depending on t,r, with arithmetic and comparisons on weights counted at unit cost as in the source. No bounded maximum degree, excluded biclique, or supplied graph decomposition is assumed. This is polynomial time for each fixed t,r, not necessarily a fixed-parameter bound f(t,r)n^C with universal C.
cards.answer_criterion: Give such an exact polynomial-time algorithm for every fixed t,r, or refute the universal algorithmic assertion, for example by an appropriate conditional hardness result for one fixed pair. Approximation or an algorithm requiring an additional bounded-degree or biclique exclusion promise does not establish the conjecture.

context_blocks.title: A long claw is an induced branching pattern
context_blocks.text: For t=1, S_{t,t,t} is the ordinary four-vertex claw K_{1,3}. Increasing t allows longer arms. Edges between selected arm vertices can destroy an induced copy, so the exclusion is different from forbidding the tree as any subgraph.

context_blocks.title: The known theorem assumes more sparsity
context_blocks.text: The source proves polynomial-time maximum-weight independent set when S_{t,t,t} is excluded as an induced subgraph and some fixed complete bipartite graph K_{s,s} is excluded as a subgraph. The conjecture asks to retain only a bound on clique size.

context_blocks.title: Small cliques do not force few edges
context_blocks.text: For t≥2, arbitrarily large complete bipartite graphs satisfy these induced-tree and triangle exclusions while having quadratically many edges. The conjectured class therefore extends beyond the sparse graph setting of the proved result.

context_blocks.title: The output is an exact optimum
context_blocks.text: Weights can make a smaller independent set preferable to a larger one. The target is the maximum sum of weights, not only the maximum number of mutually nonadjacent vertices.

cards.title: A general 3/2 communication lower bound for reliable broadcast
cards.formal: Must every Byzantine reliable-broadcast protocol in the source’s asynchronous authenticated point-to-point model have worst-case large-message communication overhead at least 3/2 asymptotically, when n=3t+1 and up to t parties can be Byzantine, even without a three-round delivery bound or a sublinear-in-n first-round sender load? This selects the source’s version with both restrictions removed.
cards.why: Would settle the leading bandwidth cost of reliable broadcast, a primitive used inside many fault-tolerant distributed protocols.
cards.status_note: Original restrictions and overhead definition checked against MiniCast, the October 2025 full follow-up and the OPODIS 2025 failure-case paper. No general lower-bound resolution was located through 12 September 2026. The question here concerns the unrestricted asynchronous version, not an unrestricted synchronous crash-fault claim.

cards.definitions: There are n=3t+1 parties with pairwise authenticated channels and a designated sender holding a message m of ℓ bits. Honest-to-honest messages are eventually delivered, with no upper bound on delay; Byzantine parties may deviate arbitrarily. Validity requires every honest party eventually to deliver m when the sender is honest. Agreement requires all honest deliveries to have the same value. Integrity allows each honest party at most one delivery, and totality requires that if one honest party delivers, all honest parties eventually do so. A Byzantine sender may cause no delivery. Let C_A(n,ℓ) be the worst-case total number of bits sent by honest parties in one execution of protocol A, over admissible inputs, faults and delivery schedules. Faulty-party transmissions are not charged. For a faulty sender, the source measures the effective message length by the largest payload fragment an honest party sends under the protocol’s declared encoding. The large-message overhead is L_A(n)=lim_{ℓ→∞} C_A(n,ℓ)/(nℓ), when the limit exists. The proposed bound is liminf_{t→∞}L_A(3t+1)≥3/2; equivalently, no constant improvement below 3/2 is possible uniformly for all sufficiently large n and sufficiently long messages. The source permits collision-resistant hashing and, for signature-based protocols, signature setup, counting their transmitted bits through a security parameter κ. The payload comparison discards lower-order terms in ℓ, such as O(κn²log n), and uses the source’s cryptographic correctness convention. There is no bound of three on the number of rounds and no restriction that the sender’s first-round total be o(nℓ).
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the universal 3/2 lower bound in the stated unrestricted asynchronous model, or give a correct protocol with a strictly smaller asymptotic worst-case payload coefficient. An upper bound of 3/2 or a lower bound only for three-round, weakly balanced protocols does not resolve this question.

context_blocks.title: The coefficient matters after linear scaling is known
context_blocks.text: Sending an ℓ-bit payload to n parties naturally costs on the order of nℓ bits. The open question concerns the leading constant caused by fault tolerance, rather than whether communication can be linear in payload length.

context_blocks.title: Two restrictions remain in the known lower bound
context_blocks.text: The original theorem applies even to synchronous crash faults, but requires delivery within three rounds and only o(nℓ) first-round bits from the sender. It does not establish the lower bound for protocols that use more rounds or concentrate the load on the sender.

context_blocks.title: Matching upper bounds now exist
context_blocks.text: MiniCast attains leading coefficient 3/2 in the worst case. The later Locher–Shoup work reduces its good-case latency to three rounds and also gives signature-based two-round variants. These constructions strengthen the evidence for optimality but do not prove the general lower bound.

context_blocks.title: Failure-free behavior is not the objective
context_blocks.text: A protocol may use approximately nℓ bits when everything goes well and still need 1.5nℓ bits in its worst execution. The conjecture is about the latter, counting all communication sent by honest parties even when a faulty sender prevents delivery.

cards.title: Fully polynomial learning of positive ReLU networks under Gaussian inputs
cards.formal: Is there a randomized learner with sample complexity and running time poly(d,k,1/ε) that, from noiseless independent examples (X,F(X)) with X∼N(0,I_d), learns every function F(x)=Σ_{i=1}^k w_i max{0,v_i·x}, where ||v_i||₂=1, w_i≥0 and Σ_i w_i≤1, to L₂ error at most ε with probability at least 9/10? The learner may be improper and must also output an efficiently evaluable hypothesis.
cards.why: Would determine whether a basic shallow neural-network class can be learned efficiently as both its dimension and width grow, without favorable assumptions on its hidden parameters.
cards.status_note: The source’s network normalization, Gaussian sample model, L₂ criterion and positive-weight question were checked, along with the earlier positive-weight theorem and later-result searches through 12 September 2026. No fully polynomial learner or matching general hardness resolution was located.

cards.definitions: The ambient dimension d and number k of hidden ReLU units are positive integers supplied as bounds to the learner; 0<ε<1 is the desired accuracy. The activation ReLU(z)=max{0,z} has no bias or threshold shift here. The hidden unit vectors v_i and output coefficients w_i are unknown. Positivity concerns the output coefficients w_i, not the coordinates of v_i. The learner receives fresh i.i.d. samples from the stated distribution, not queries at chosen inputs. Its output H:R^d→R succeeds when (E_{X∼N(0,I_d)}[(H(X)−F(X))²])^{1/2}≤ε. The probability of at least 9/10 is over both samples and learner randomness; the error expectation uses a fresh Gaussian input. A single polynomial must bound sample count, running time, output-description size and evaluation cost as d,k,1/ε vary; k is not fixed. As in the source, examples have real coordinates and complexity is the arithmetic/sample complexity of the learning model, not an asserted finite-bit bound for exact Gaussian observations. H need not itself have k ReLU units. There is no separation, rank, conditioning or identifiability assumption on the v_i. Zero coefficients simply allow fewer than k active units.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct a learner satisfying the simultaneous polynomial dependence on d,k,1/ε for all normalized nonnegative-weight targets, or establish a valid hardness obstruction to that guarantee in the same sample-access model. A result only for fixed k, well-separated parameters, proper learning, or a restricted query algorithm does not resolve the full question.

context_blocks.title: The task is prediction rather than parameter recovery
context_blocks.text: Different hidden networks can represent the same or nearly the same function. The learner only needs to predict F accurately on new Gaussian inputs; it need not reconstruct the original hidden vectors.

context_blocks.title: The dependence on width is the open issue
context_blocks.text: A running time such as (dk/ε)^{O(k)} is polynomial when k is fixed, but its exponent grows with the width. The requested fully polynomial learner must use a fixed exponent even as the number of hidden units grows.

cards.context:
Different hidden networks can represent the same or nearly the same function. The learner only needs to predict F accurately on new Gaussian inputs; it need not reconstruct the original hidden vectors.

A running time such as (dk/ε)^{O(k)} is polynomial when k is fixed, but its exponent grows with the width. The requested fully polynomial learner must use a fixed exponent even as the number of hidden units grows.

The cited positive-weight algorithm runs in poly(dk/ε)+(k/ε)^{O(log²k)} time. This is quasipolynomial rather than polynomial in k and inverse accuracy. The 2024 source explicitly leaves the fully polynomial version open even in this special case.

The 2024 paper discusses lower bounds for correlational statistical queries in the broader signed-weight class. Those bounds do not by themselves rule out a sample-based learner for this positive-weight question, and the learner here is not restricted to correlation queries.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.

benchmark_selection.basis: Individual editorial review of saved titles, importance rationales, problem statements, source notes and working summaries. This is a review of importance and topical diversity, not a fresh verification of open status or completion of draft formulations. Importance scores are preserved.
